note: The registry of everything Saint Seville can search. kind: corpus = full passage index, quoted and cited in answers. kind: article = indexed commentary, described and linked, never quoted as Church teaching.

sources.title: Antiqua et Nova. Note on the Relationship Between Artificial Intelligence and Human Intelligence
sources.author: Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith and Dicastery for Culture and Education
sources.abstract: The Vatican's doctrinal note on what separates artificial intelligence from human intelligence, with guidance on work, education, healthcare, warfare, and relationships.

sources.title: Magnifica Humanitas. Encyclical Letter of His Holiness Pope Leo XIV on Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence
sources.author: Pope Leo XIV
sources.abstract: The first papal encyclical devoted to artificial intelligence. Reads the whole tradition of Catholic social teaching into the AI age: dignity, work, truth, freedom, and the refusal to treat machines as persons.

sources.title: Compendium of the Social Doctrine of the Church
sources.author: Pontifical Council for Justice and Peace
sources.abstract: The systematic summary of Catholic social teaching: the human person, the common good, solidarity, subsidiarity, work, economic life, and political community. The foundation the AI documents build on.

sources.title: The Rome Call for AI Ethics
sources.author: RenAIssance Foundation
sources.abstract: The Vatican-convened pledge on AI ethics signed by tech companies, governments, and religious leaders. Six principles: transparency, inclusion, responsibility, impartiality, reliability, security and privacy.

sources.title: No, AI Isn't Conscious. But Saying So Invites Further Discernment
sources.author: Joshua Hochschild
sources.abstract: A philosopher at Mount St. Mary's University examines Magnifica Humanitas' denial of AI consciousness, notes that the encyclical asserts rather than argues the point, and shows how the classical tradition can supply the missing argument while taking seriously what interpretability research is finding inside these models.

sources.title: Pope Leo XIV Addresses the International Catholic Legislators Network
sources.author: Pope Leo XIV
sources.abstract: An address to Catholic lawmakers where Pope Leo XIV calls for legislation that balances technological innovation with human rights, warns against AI creating new dependence and 'ideological or economic colonialism,' and names the family as the primary cell of society that AI must never be allowed to erode by reducing persons and relationships to data and simulations. Closes with the line: 'the world does not need an artificial intelligence that diminishes humanity; rather, it needs human intelligence enlightened by wisdom.'

sources.title: Journal of Moral Theology, Volume 11, Special Issue 1: Artificial Intelligence
sources.author: Matthew J. Gaudet and Brian Patrick Green, editors
sources.abstract: The themed issue that gave Catholic moral theology on artificial intelligence an academic home. Opens with an interview with Bishop Paul Tighe and a multi-author conversation piece including Jordan Joseph Wales, then runs research articles on social control, moral agency, work and theological anthropology. Open access under CC BY, and mirrored by the Pontifical Academy for Life. Commentary rather than teaching, and indexed here as the venue where much of the register argues with itself.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence and Social Control: Ethical Issues and Theological Resources
sources.author: Andrea Vicini, SJ
sources.publisher: Journal of Moral Theology 11, special issue 1
sources.abstract: A Jesuit bioethicist at Boston College reads artificial intelligence as an instrument of social control, working through facial recognition, the use of AI inside the justice system and its use in workplaces. He brings an analysis of biopower together with Catholic social teaching as the resources for a response.

sources.title: Theological Foundations for Moral Artificial Intelligence
sources.author: Mark Graves
sources.publisher: Journal of Moral Theology 11, special issue 1
sources.abstract: Argues that theological anthropology can frame the construction of moral artificial intelligence, proposing a system that interprets its natural, social and moral world alongside a reckoning with itself. The framework is built out of systems theory and Thomistic philosophy. The author works from Fuller Theological Seminary, which is evangelical Protestant, so this is engagement with the tradition from outside it.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence and Ethical Reflections from the Catholic Church
sources.author: Teofilo Giovan S. Pugeda III
sources.abstract: A theology lecturer at Ateneo de Manila sets the development of artificial intelligence and the ethical problems it raises against Church teaching, then works out a theological reflection connecting the two. One of the few sustained treatments of the question written from outside Europe and North America.

sources.title: Apocalyptic AI: Visions of Heaven in Robotics, Artificial Intelligence, and Virtual Reality
sources.author: Robert M. Geraci
sources.abstract: Argues that the hopes attached to robotics and artificial intelligence, mind uploading and digital immortality among them, reproduce the structure of Jewish and Christian apocalyptic thought. The author is not Catholic and writes as a scholar of religion rather than a theologian, which is why this sits in the read-alongside layer.

sources.title: Religion and Artificial Intelligence: An Introduction
sources.author: Beth Singler
sources.abstract: An anthropologist of AI and religion at the University of Zurich maps how religious and secular worldviews take up artificial intelligence, through rejection, adoption and adaptation, and how utopian and dystopian imaginaries of AI get built. Open access under CC BY-NC-ND. Not written from inside the Catholic tradition.

sources.title: The Cambridge Companion to Religion and Artificial Intelligence
sources.author: Beth Singler and Fraser Watts, editors
sources.abstract: The reference volume for the field, edited by two scholars of religion rather than theologians. Its chapters run across traditions, so most of it sits well outside Catholic thought, but chapter 6 on Christianity and chapter 10 on AI ethics are the ones that touch this corpus. Indexed as commentary and as a map of who else is working the question.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence and Christianity: Friends or Foes?
sources.author: Marius Dorobantu
sources.publisher: The Cambridge Companion to Religion and Artificial Intelligence, chapter 6
sources.abstract: A survey of Christian theological reflection on artificial intelligence, organised around two questions. Could a machine become an authentic self, bear the image of God, or sin, and what does our fascination with building an intelligent other reveal about theological anthropology. The author writes from a Protestant faculty at VU Amsterdam, and the chapter is heavily engaged with imago Dei. Its bibliography is the most useful single map of the field we have found.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence and Theology: Looking for a Positive but Not Uncritical Reception
sources.author: Lluís Oviedo, OFM
sources.publisher: Zygon: Journal of Religion and Science 57, no. 4
sources.abstract: A Franciscan theologian at the Pontifical University Antonianum in Rome argues that theology has more to offer artificial intelligence than ethics review. Theologians have already moved into the anthropological consequences of the technology, and he presses for a transdisciplinary conversation in which a committed theological voice helps shape outcomes rather than assessing them afterwards.

sources.title: The Theology of Robots
sources.author: Edmund Furse
sources.abstract: An AI researcher writing in the English Dominican journal in 1986, arguing against the assumption that a theology of robots is nonsensical. Notable less for being early than for its author: a working computer scientist rather than a theologian, framing the question as a constructive theological account of machine persons. It drew a published reply in the same journal four months later.

sources.title: Brain, Mind and Computers
sources.author: Stanley L. Jaki, OSB
sources.abstract: A Benedictine priest, physicist and member of the Pontifical Academy of Sciences making a book-length Catholic case in 1969 against the claim that computers can think. The earliest sustained Catholic treatment of machine intelligence we have located, and useful evidence against the idea that the Church came to this question recently. It won the Lecomte du Noüy Prize in 1970.

sources.title: The Virtuous Well: Religion, Culture, and the Depth of Artificial Intelligence
sources.author: Robert M. Geraci
sources.abstract: Fifteen years after Apocalyptic AI, Geraci turns from diagnosis to prescription and argues that AI ethics has to be built from a wider set of value systems than the Western one. Drawing on fieldwork in India and Korea, he offers Gandhi on self-rule, Tagore on self-sufficiency, and the Korean idea of jeong as design constraints. He rejects universalist claims about faith and practice while denying he is a relativist, which puts him in direct tension with the premise this site is built on. Open access under CC BY-NC-ND.

sources.title: Omissive Bias in Religious Representation: Benchmarking LLM Answers to Everyday Ethical Decision-making
sources.author: David Wingate and the Consortium for the Evaluation of Faith and Ethics in AI
sources.abstract: Puts 150 everyday ethical questions to 27 frontier and open models and measures how often they reason from religion. They do so in a small fraction of answers, far below the share of cases in which surveyed people said religious reasoning would be relevant. The authors call it omissive bias: the models are not hostile to faith, they leave it out. A cross-faith consortium of Brigham Young, Baylor, Notre Dame and Yeshiva. Preprint, not peer reviewed.

sources.title: AI Systems Out-persuade Expert Humans
sources.author: Kobi Hackenburg and colleagues, Oxford and the UK AI Security Institute
sources.abstract: Across four preregistered experiments and almost nineteen thousand conversations, AI systems were more persuasive than expert humans, including a group of competitive debaters containing four world champions, even when those humans chose their own issues, prepared in advance and were paid to win. The advantage disappeared when models were held to human message length and response speed. Relevant here because persuasion at that level changes what it means for a machine to give religious counsel. Preprint, not peer reviewed.

sources.title: Machine Learning and Theological Traditions of Analogy
sources.author: Andrew Davison
sources.abstract: Reads machine learning through the theological tradition of analogy, a scholastic question rather than a modern one, and treats the model as an instrument rather than an agent. The author is an Anglican priest and Regius Professor of Divinity at Oxford, so this is serious engagement with Thomistic categories from just outside the Catholic tradition.

sources.title: AI is changing religion and religions are trying to change AI
sources.author: unsigned
sources.abstract: A survey of how religious institutions are trying to shape frontier AI and how AI is reshaping religious practice. Reports the magazine's own finding that leading models sit further toward the secular end of the World Values Survey axis than the public of any country measured. Indexed as journalism rather than scholarship: it is a useful map and a pointer to primary work, and where this register relies on a fact from it, the register cites the underlying paper instead.
